sections.title: Introduction to Electrostatics
sections.narration: Welcome to our study of electrostatics! This fascinating branch of physics governs everything from the spark you feel on a dry day to the forces that hold atoms themselves together. In this series, we'll journey into the world of stationary electric charges. We will uncover the fundamental laws that describe how they interact, the fields they create, and the potential energy stored within these systems. Understanding electrostatics is the first crucial step to mastering electricity and magnetism, concepts that are the bedrock of modern technology. So, let's begin our exploration of the invisible, yet immensely powerful, world of electric charge.

sections.title: What You'll Learn in This Video
sections.narration: In this first lesson, we will lay the groundwork for our entire study of electrostatics. First, we’ll define what electricity is and break it down into its three main areas of study: electrostatics, which deals with fixed charges; electric current, the study of moving charges; and electromagnetism, which unites them both. Then, we will dive into the heart of the matter: the concept of charge itself. We'll learn that all charge comes in two, and only two, types: positive and negative. We'll explore what it means for an object to be neutral. Finally, we'll connect this to the atomic world, understanding how the simple act of adding or removing tiny electrons is what makes an object electrically charged. By the end, you'll have a solid foundation for the more advanced topics to come.

sections.title: The Three Branches of Electricity
sections.narration: At its core, electricity is all about a fundamental property of matter called charge. The entire classical study of electricity can be neatly organized into three main areas, each focusing on a different aspect of charge's behavior. First, we have Electrostatics, which is the focus of this chapter. This is the study of charges that are not moving. Think of a balloon sticking to a wall after you've rubbed it on your hair—the forces between these fixed, static charges are what electrostatics is all about. The second area is Electric Current. This is what most people think of as 'electricity'—the flow of charge. It deals with circuits, power, and the energy associated with charges in motion, like electrons moving through a wire to light a bulb. Finally, we have Electromagnetism. This is the most comprehensive of the three, studying the forces that arise between charges that are in motion. It turns out that moving charges create magnetic fields, and changing magnetic fields can make charges move. This deep connection is the principle behind electric motors, generators, and even light itself. For now, we will concentrate on the first and most fundamental area: electrostatics.

sections.title: Positive, Negative, and Neutral
sections.narration: So, what is this 'charge' we keep talking about? Electric charge is a fundamental, built-in property of matter. After countless experiments, we've found that it comes in two, and only two, types. The names for these were chosen by Benjamin Franklin, and while the choice was completely arbitrary, the convention has stuck. We call them positive and negative. A key rule to remember is that like charges repel each other, while opposite charges attract. So, two positive charges will push each other away, as will two negative charges. But a positive and a negative charge will pull towards each other. Now, what about objects that aren't charged, like a wooden block just sitting there? We call these objects 'neutral'. This doesn't mean they lack charge altogether. In fact, a neutral object has a vast number of charges, but it contains an exactly equal amount of positive and negative charge. These opposite charges cancel each other out on a large scale, resulting in no net electric force. So, 'neutral' isn't a third type of charge; it's a state of perfect balance between the two types that do exist.

segments.text: So, what is this 'charge' we keep talking about? Electric charge is a fundamental, built-in property of matter. After countless experiments, we've found that it comes in two, and only two, types.
The names for these were chosen by Benjamin Franklin, and while the choice was completely arbitrary, the convention has stuck. We call them positive and negative.
A key rule to remember is that like charges repel each other, while opposite charges attract. So, two positive charges will push each other away, as will two negative charges.
But a positive and a negative charge will pull towards each other.
Now, what about objects that aren't charged, like a wooden block just sitting there? We call these objects 'neutral'. This doesn't mean they lack charge altogether.

In fact, a neutral object has a vast number of charges, but it contains an exactly equal amount of positive and negative charge. These opposite charges cancel each other out on a large scale, resulting in no net electric force.
So, 'neutral' isn't a third type of charge; it's a state of perfect balance between the two types that do exist.

sections.title: How Objects Become Charged
sections.narration: If neutral objects contain balanced positive and negative charges, how does an object become charged? The answer lies in the structure of the atom. Atoms are normally electrically neutral, containing an equal number of positive protons in the nucleus and negative electrons orbiting that nucleus. The protons are locked tightly in the center, but the electrons, especially the outermost ones, can sometimes be transferred from one atom to another. This is the key: charge is transferred by moving electrons. If a body gains extra electrons, it will have more negative charges than positive charges. Conventionally, we say this body is now negatively charged. Conversely, if a body loses some of its electrons, it will be left with an excess of positive protons in its nuclei. This results in a net positive charge, and we say the body is positively charged. So, when you rub a glass rod with silk, you aren't creating charge. You are simply moving electrons from the glass to the silk. The glass, having lost electrons, becomes positive. The silk, having gained those same electrons, becomes negative. The total charge remains the same, it's just been separated.

sections.title: Introduction to Coulomb's Law
sections.narration: Welcome! Today, we delve into one of the fundamental principles of electrostatics: Coulomb's Law. Imagine you have two tiny, charged objects, which we call point charges. How do they interact? Coulomb's Law gives us the answer. It states that the force between these two point charges is directly proportional to the product of their magnitudes. This means if you double the charge of one, the force between them also doubles. If you double both, the force quadruples! At the same time, this force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. This is a crucial relationship known as an inverse square law. If you double the distance between the charges, the force doesn't just get halved; it becomes four times weaker. Triple the distance, and the force becomes nine times weaker. This rapid drop-off with distance is a key characteristic of electrostatic forces. Finally, the direction of this force is always along the straight line connecting the two charges. If the charges are alike—both positive or both negative—they repel each other, pushing each other away along that line. If they are opposite—one positive and one negative—they attract, pulling each other closer along that same line. This force is also conservative, which means the work done by it in moving a charge between two points is independent of the path taken.

sections.title: The Coulomb's Law Formula
sections.narration: Now that we understand the relationships, let's put them together into a precise mathematical formula. We combine the two proportionalities, F is proportional to the product of charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance, into a single expression: F is proportional to q₁q₂ divided by r-squared. To turn this proportionality into an equation, we introduce a constant of proportionality, which we call 'k'. So, the formula for the magnitude of the force becomes F equals k times the product of q₁ and q₂ divided by r-squared. This constant 'k' is known as Coulomb's constant. In a vacuum or free space, its value is approximately 9 times 10 to the power of 9 Newton-meters-squared per Coulomb-squared. This is a very large number, indicating that electrostatic forces are inherently very strong. The constant k can also be expressed in terms of another fundamental constant called the permittivity of free space, represented by epsilon-naught (ε₀). The relationship is k equals 1 over 4 pi epsilon-naught. The value of epsilon-naught is about 8.85 times 10 to the power of minus 12 Coulombs-squared per Newton-meter-squared. Understanding these constants is key to applying Coulomb's law in different scenarios, especially when we move charges out of a vacuum and into other materials.

sections.title: The Effect of a Medium
sections.narration: So far, we've only considered charges in a vacuum. But what happens if we place them in a different material, like water, oil, or glass? The presence of a medium changes the electrostatic force between the charges. The medium itself contains atoms and molecules that can be polarized by the electric field of our charges. This polarization creates an opposing electric field, which effectively weakens the original force. We account for this by modifying Coulomb's law. Instead of just epsilon-naught, we use the permittivity of the medium, which is epsilon-naught multiplied by a new quantity, epsilon-r (εᵣ), known as the relative permittivity or the dielectric constant of the medium, often denoted by 'K'. This value tells us how much the force is reduced compared to a vacuum. So the new formula becomes F_medium equals 1 over 4 pi epsilon-naught epsilon-r times q1q2 over r-squared. Since the force in a vacuum is F_vac equals 1 over 4 pi epsilon-naught times the charge part, we can see that the force in the medium is simply the force in vacuum divided by the dielectric constant, K. For a vacuum, K is 1. For water, K is about 80, meaning the force between two charges in water is 80 times weaker than in a vacuum! For metals, K is considered infinite, which means the electrostatic force inside a conductor is zero. This effect is crucial in many applications, from capacitor design to understanding chemical reactions in solutions.

segments.text: So far, we've only considered charges in a vacuum. But what happens if we place them in a different material, like water, oil, or glass? The presence of a medium changes the electrostatic force between the charges.

The medium itself contains atoms and molecules that can be polarized by the electric field of our charges. This polarization creates an opposing electric field, which effectively weakens the original force.

We account for this by modifying Coulomb's law. Instead of just epsilon-naught, we use the permittivity of the medium, which is epsilon-naught multiplied by a new quantity, epsilon-r (εᵣ), known as the relative permittivity or the dielectric constant of the medium, often denoted by 'K'.
This value tells us how much the force is reduced compared to a vacuum. So the new formula becomes F_medium equals 1 over 4 pi epsilon-naught epsilon-r times q1q2 over r-squared.

Since the force in a vacuum is F_vac equals 1 over 4 pi epsilon-naught times the charge part, we can see that the force in the medium is simply the force in vacuum divided by the dielectric constant, K.

For a vacuum, K is 1. For water, K is about 80, meaning the force between two charges in water is 80 times weaker than in a vacuum! For metals, K is considered infinite, which means the electrostatic force inside a conductor is zero.
This effect is crucial in many applications, from capacitor design to understanding chemical reactions in solutions.

sections.title: Coulomb's Law in Vector Form
sections.narration: Force is a vector quantity, meaning it has both magnitude and direction. So far, we've focused on the magnitude, but a complete description requires vector notation. Let's set up a coordinate system. Suppose we have two charges, q₁ and q₂, located at positions described by position vectors r₁ and r₂ respectively, both originating from the origin. The vector pointing from charge q₂ to charge q₁ is given by the difference of their position vectors: r₁ minus r₂. The direction of the force is along this line. Let's find the force exerted on charge q₁ by charge q₂, which we denote as F₁₂. The magnitude is given by the formula we already know, but the distance 'r' is now the magnitude of the vector difference, |r₁ - r₂|. To give this force a direction, we multiply the magnitude by a unit vector that points from q₂ to q₁. A unit vector is found by dividing a vector by its own magnitude. So, the unit vector is (r₁ - r₂) divided by |r₁ - r₂|. Combining these, the vector force F₁₂ is k times q₁q₂ divided by the magnitude squared, all multiplied by the unit vector. This simplifies to F₁₂ equals k times q₁q₂ divided by the magnitude of (r₁ - r₂) cubed, multiplied by the vector (r₁ - r₂). This form is powerful because it automatically handles attraction and repulsion. If q₁ and q₂ have the same sign, their product is positive, and the force F₁₂ points in the same direction as (r₁ - r₂), which is away from q₂—a repulsive force. If they have opposite signs, their product is negative, and the force F₁₂ points opposite to (r₁ - r₂), which is towards q₂—an attractive force.

sections.title: The Superposition Principle
sections.narration: Coulomb's law tells us about the force between two charges. But what if we have three, four, or a whole collection of charges? This is where the powerful Superposition Principle comes into play. It states that the interaction between any two charges is completely independent of the presence of any other charges. This is a remarkable simplification. It means we can calculate the total force on one charge by considering the effect of every other charge one at a time. The net electrostatic force on a particular charge is simply the vector sum of the individual forces exerted on it by all other charges in the system. For example, if we want to find the force on a charge Q due to charges q₁, q₂, and q₃, we first use Coulomb's law to find the force F₁ exerted by q₁ on Q, ignoring q₂ and q₃. Then, we find the force F₂ exerted by q₂ on Q, ignoring q₁ and q₃. We do the same for q₃. Finally, the total resultant force F_net on charge Q is the vector sum of F₁, F₂, and F₃. Remember, this is a vector sum, not a simple addition of magnitudes. We need to consider both the magnitude and direction of each individual force. We can use techniques like breaking vectors into components or using the parallelogram law of vector addition. If we have two forces F₁ and F₂ acting on a charge at an angle theta, the magnitude of the resultant force F is given by the square root of F₁ squared plus F₂ squared plus 2 times F₁F₂ cosine theta.

sections.title: Example 2: Force in a Dielectric Medium
sections.narration: Let's work through an example. The force between two point charges placed in a vacuum is measured to be 18 Newtons. Now, a glass plate with a dielectric constant of 6 is introduced between them. What will the new electric force be? First, let's identify what we know. The initial force in a vacuum, F_vac, is 18 N. The dielectric constant of the glass, which we denote as K or epsilon_r, is 6. We need to find the new force, F_medium. We recall the relationship between the force in a vacuum and the force in a medium. The force in the medium is equal to the force in the vacuum divided by the dielectric constant of that medium. This simple formula captures the shielding effect of the material. Now we just need to substitute our values. F_medium equals 18 Newtons divided by 6. Performing the division, we find that the new force is 3 Newtons. As expected, introducing the dielectric material has significantly weakened the force between the charges, reducing it by a factor of 6.

segments.text: Let's work through an example. The force between two point charges placed in a vacuum is measured to be 18 Newtons.
Now, a glass plate with a dielectric constant of 6 is now introduced between them. What will the new electric force be?

First, let's identify what we know. The initial force in a vacuum, F_vac, is 18 N. The dielectric constant of the glass, which we denote as K or epsilon_r, is 6. We need to find the new force, F_medium.
We recall the relationship between the force in a vacuum and the force in a medium. The force in the medium is equal to the force in the vacuum divided by the dielectric constant of that medium.
Now we just need to substitute our values. F_medium equals 18 Newtons divided by 6.

Performing the division, we find that the new force is 3 Newtons. As expected, introducing the dielectric material has significantly weakened the force between the charges, reducing it by a factor of 6.

sections.title: Example 3: Forces on a Line
sections.narration: Here's a problem involving superposition. Four identical charges, each with a value of 2 microcoulombs, are placed on the x-axis at positions x = 0, 2, 4, and 8 centimeters. We want to find the total force exerted on the charge located at x = 2 centimeters. Let's analyze the forces acting on this central charge. It will experience forces from the other three charges. First, consider the charge at x=0. Since both charges are positive, the charge at x=0 will exert a repulsive force on our target charge, pushing it to the right. Now, consider the charge at x=4 cm. This charge is also positive and is the same distance away from our target charge as the one at x=0, but on the opposite side. Therefore, it will exert a repulsive force of the exact same magnitude, but this time pushing to the left. These two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel each other out completely. The resultant force from these two is zero. This means the only force we need to calculate is the one exerted by the charge at x = 8 cm. The distance 'r' between the charge at 2 cm and the charge at 8 cm is 6 cm, which is 0.06 meters. The charges q₁ and q₂ are both 2 microcoulombs, or 2 times 10 to the minus 6 Coulombs. Using Coulomb's Law, F equals k q₁q₂ over r-squared, we substitute the values: F equals (9 times 10⁹) times (2 times 10⁻⁶) times (2 times 10⁻⁶), all divided by (0.06) squared. This calculation gives us a final force of 10 Newtons.

sections.title: Example 4: Smallest Electric Force
sections.narration: Let's consider a fascinating question: What is the smallest possible electric force between two charges placed 1.0 meter apart? To answer this, we need to think about the components of Coulomb's Law: F equals k times q₁q₂ over r-squared. We are given a fixed distance, r = 1.0 meter, and k is a constant. So, to make the force F as small as possible, the product of the charges, q₁q₂, must be at its minimum possible value. What is the smallest unit of charge that can exist freely? It's the elementary charge, 'e', the magnitude of the charge on a single electron or proton. The value of 'e' is approximately 1.6 times 10 to the power of minus 19 Coulombs. Therefore, the minimum possible values for q₁ and q₂ are both equal to 'e'. Now we can substitute these minimum values into our formula. The minimum force, F_min, will be k, which is 9 times 10⁹, multiplied by the product of the two elementary charges, (1.6 times 10⁻¹⁹) times (1.6 times 10⁻¹⁹), all divided by the distance squared, which is (1.0)². After performing the multiplication, we find that the smallest possible electric force at this distance is 2.304 times 10 to the power of minus 28 Newtons. This is an incredibly tiny force, illustrating just how small the elementary charge is.

sections.title: Example 5: Force Using Position Vectors
sections.narration: Let's tackle a problem using the vector form of Coulomb's Law. We have two point charges, A and B. Charge A is 1/2 Coulomb and its position vector is (i + j + k). Charge B is 2 Coulombs and its position vector is (-i - j + 3k). We need to find the force exerted on charge A by charge B, which we'll call F_AB. First, we write down our knowns: q_A, q_B, r_A, and r_B. The vector form of Coulomb's Law for the force on A due to B is F_AB equals k times q_A q_B, divided by the magnitude of the vector from B to A cubed, all multiplied by the vector from B to A itself. The vector from B to A is r_A minus r_B. Let's calculate this first. (i + j + k) minus (-i - j + 3k) gives us (2i + 2j - 2k). Next, we need the magnitude of this vector. The magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squares of its components: square root of (2² + 2² + (-2)²), which is the square root of (4 + 4 + 4) or the square root of 12. So the magnitude cubed is (sqrt(12))³. Now we can plug everything into our formula. F_AB equals (9 times 10⁹) times (1/2 times 2), divided by (sqrt(12))³, all multiplied by the vector (2i + 2j - 2k). The charge product is simply 1. Simplifying the denominator and the vector gives us our final answer in vector form. This process shows how the vector formula directly gives us both the magnitude and direction of the force in a 3D space.

segments.text: Let's tackle a problem using the vector form of Coulomb's Law. We have two point charges, A and B. Charge A is 1/2 Coulomb and its position vector is (i + j + k). Charge B is 2 Coulombs and its position vector is (-i - j + 3k).
We need to find the force exerted on charge A by charge B, which we'll call F_AB. First, we write down our knowns: q_A, q_B, r_A, and r_B.
The vector form of Coulomb's Law for the force on A due to B is F_AB equals k times q_A q_B, divided by the magnitude of the vector from B to A cubed, all multiplied by the vector from B to A itself.
The vector from B to A is r_A minus r_B. Let's calculate this first. (i + j + k) minus (-i - j + 3k) gives us (2i + 2j - 2k).

Next, we need the magnitude of this vector. The magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squares of its components: square root of (2² + 2² + (-2)²), which is the square root of (4 + 4 + 4) or the square root of 12.
So the magnitude cubed is (sqrt(12))³. Now we can plug everything into our formula. F_AB equals (9 times 10⁹) times (1/2 times 2), divided by (sqrt(12))³, all multiplied by the vector (2i + 2j - 2k).

The charge product is simply 1. Simplifying the denominator and the vector gives us our final answer in vector form. This process shows how the vector formula directly gives us both the magnitude and direction of the force in a 3D space.

sections.title: Example 6: Charges on an Equilateral Triangle
sections.narration: Let's consider a symmetric arrangement. Three equal positive charges, Q, are placed on the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side length 'a'. Our goal is to find the resultant force on any one of these charges due to the other two. Let's focus on the charge at the top vertex. It will experience two separate forces: one from the charge at the bottom-left vertex, and one from the charge at the bottom-right vertex. Let's call these forces F₁ and F₂. Since all charges are equal (Q) and all distances are the same (side length 'a'), the magnitudes of these two forces will be identical. Using Coulomb's Law, the magnitude of both F₁ and F₂ is k times Q-squared divided by a-squared. Now, what about the direction? The force F₁ from the bottom-left charge will be repulsive, pushing the top charge up and to the right. The force F₂ from the bottom-right charge will also be repulsive, pushing the top charge up and to the left. The angle between these two force vectors is the same as the angle at the vertex of an equilateral triangle, which is 60 degrees. To find the resultant force, we use the law of cosines for vector addition: the magnitude of the net force F is the square root of (F₁² + F₂² + 2F₁F₂cos(60°)). Since F₁ equals F₂, we can substitute F₁ for F₂. Knowing that cos(60°) is 1/2, the equation simplifies to the square root of (F₁² + F₁² + 2F₁² times 1/2), which is the square root of 3F₁². This gives us a final resultant force magnitude of F₁ times the square root of 3. Substituting the expression for F₁, the net force is the square root of 3 times kQ² over a².

sections.narration: Let's look at Case I. Three particles in a line, with net forces pointing away from the center. For the outer particles to be pushed outwards, the charges must be repulsive. Let's assume they are all positive. The middle charge would be repelled by both outer charges, so the net force on it should be zero if they are symmetric. The diagram shows a non-zero force, making Case I impossible. Now, Case II. The outer particles are repelled, but the middle one is attracted. This is possible if the outer charges are positive and the middle one is negative. The net forces shown are consistent with this arrangement. So, Case II is possible. In Case III, three charges in a triangle all repel each other. This is perfectly fine if all three charges have the same sign, for example, all positive. The forces would push them apart as shown. So, Case III is also possible. Finally, Case IV shows repulsive forces in a triangle, but the force vectors are not symmetric, which they should be for an equilateral arrangement of identical charges. Also, they seem to violate the principle that the vector sum of forces in a closed system under only internal interactions should be zero. Thus, Case IV is incorrect. Therefore, situations II and III are the only correct ones.

sections.title: Practice Problem 2: Calculation
sections.narration: Let's define a base force F = kQq/d^2. For case I, P is at distance d, 2d, and 3d from three positive charges. All forces are repulsive (to the right). The net force is F_I = kQq/d^2 + kQq/(2d)^2 + kQq/(3d)^2 = F * (1 + 1/4 + 1/9) ≈ 1.36F. For case II, P is between two positive charges and a negative one. The two +Q charges are at distance d and 2d, and the -Q is at distance d. The forces are: repulsive from left +Q (rightward), repulsive from middle +Q (leftward), and attractive to right -Q (rightward). So, F_II = F/d^2 - F/(2d)^2 + F/d^2 = F * (1 - 1/4 + 1) = 1.75F. For case III, P is at distances d, 2d, 3d from charges +Q, +Q, -Q. The forces are: repulsive from the two +Q (rightward) and attractive to -Q (leftward). So, F_III = F/(2d)^2 + F/(3d)^2 - F/d^2 = F * (1/4 + 1/9 - 1) = -0.64F. The magnitude is 0.64F. For case IV, P is at distances d, 2d, 3d from charges +Q, -Q, +Q. sections.title: Practice Problem 4: Electric vs Gravitational Force
sections.narration: This question asks for the order of magnitude of the ratio of the electric force to the gravitational force between two electrons. This is a classic comparison that highlights the incredible strength of the electric force. First, we write down the formula for the electric force between two electrons, which is F_e = k * e^2 / r^2. Then, we write the formula for the gravitational force, F_g = G * m_e^2 / r^2, where m_e is the mass of an electron. To find the ratio, we divide F_e by F_g. Notice that the distance squared term, r^2, cancels out. The ratio is independent of the distance between the electrons! Now we just need to plug in the constants: k, the Coulomb constant; e, the elementary charge; G, the gravitational constant; and m_e, the mass of the electron.

sections.title: Introduction to the Electric Field
sections.narration: So far, we've talked about forces between charges that are some distance apart. This might seem strange, like 'action at a distance'. How does one charge 'know' the other is there? To explain this, the great physicist Michael Faraday introduced the concept of a field. The idea is that a charge doesn't directly pull on another charge far away. Instead, it modifies the space around itself. This modification of space is called an electric field. Think of it like a massive object like the Sun. The Sun creates a gravitational field that extends throughout the solar system. The Earth doesn't get pulled by the Sun directly; it responds to the gravitational field at its location. It's the same with charges. A source charge creates an electric field. Then, if you place another charge, called a test charge, into this field, the field exerts a force on it. The field is the intermediary. We define the strength and direction of this field, called the Electric Field Intensity, E, as the force F experienced by a small positive test charge q, divided by the magnitude of that test charge itself. So, E equals F over q. The field is a vector quantity, pointing in the direction of the force on a positive charge. This powerful concept allows us to describe the electrical environment at any point in space, created by any arrangement of charges.

sections.narration: Let's review the key concepts from this chapter with some flashcards. Try to answer the question before the reveal. What is electrostatics? It's the study of forces, fields, and potentials from static charges. What is the principle of conservation of charge? The net charge of an isolated system remains constant. What is the principle of quantization of charge? Charge exists in discrete packets, q = Ne, where N is an integer. What is Coulomb's Law? It describes the force between two point charges: F = k * q1 * q2 / r^2. What are the three main methods of charging an object? Friction, conduction, and induction. What is the true test of electrification? Repulsion, because a charged body can attract a neutral one. What does a stationary charge produce? An electric field. What does a charge in constant velocity motion produce? Both an electric and a magnetic field. What is the definition of the Electric Field vector E? It's the force per unit charge, E = F/q.

sections.title: Chapter Recap: The Story of Charge
sections.narration: Let's recap the story of electrostatics. Our journey began inside the atom, with protons and electrons, the fundamental carriers of positive and negative charge. We saw that by adding or removing electrons, we could turn neutral objects into charged ones. We learned that charge is conserved—it can't be created or destroyed, only moved around. And it's quantized, coming in tiny packets of size 'e'. Then, we witnessed these charges interacting. We uncovered Coulomb's Law, the rule that governs their attraction and repulsion, a force that depends powerfully on distance. We saw how to add these forces like arrows using the principle of superposition. We explored the different ways to charge objects: by rubbing them together, by direct contact, or by simply bringing a charge nearby to induce a separation of charges. Finally, to solve the puzzle of 'action at a distance', we were introduced to the electric field—an invisible influence that a charge creates in the space around it, telling other charges how to move. This field is the true messenger of the electrostatic force, setting the stage for all the electrical phenomena we will explore next.
